html:
The Wadai Sultanate was a Muslim state east of Lake Chad, in what is now eastern Chad, shown on the map from 1530 to 1800. Before about 1635 the region was ruled by the Tunjur kings; that year Abd al-Karim, a Muslim leader of the Maba people, overthrew them and founded the sultanate.

Wadai sat between two larger neighbours, Darfur to the east and Kanem-Bornu to the west, and fought both. It raided the lands to its south, including Bagirmi, for captives.

In the 1800s it grew strong under Sultan Muhammad Sharif and his successors. A desert route north through the oases of Kufra to Benghazi on the Mediterranean, protected by the Senusiyya Sufi order, made Wadai a major player in the late trans-Saharan trade in ivory and enslaved people. France conquered its capital, Abéché, in 1909 and finished the conquest by 1912, adding Wadai to French Equatorial Africa.
